title: Forms: Collecting User Input 📝
description: Meet the `<form>` element and essential controls like `<input>` and `<label>`.

slides.title: The Role of HTML Forms 📬
slides.content:
# How Users Send You Data

Forms are the backbone of interactivity: login pages, search bars, contact forms, checkout. They collect input and send it to a server (or process it locally with JavaScript).

A form is wrapped in the `<form>` element:
```html
<form action="/submit" method="post">
  <!-- form controls go here -->
</form>
```
We'll explore `action` and `method` later; right now focus on the controls.

slides.title: The Mighty `<input>` Tag 🆎
slides.content:
# One Tag, Many Faces

`<input>` is a void element whose behaviour changes dramatically based on its `type` attribute.

Basic types:
- `text` – single line text (default).
- `password` – masked text.
- `email` – optimized for email addresses.
- `number` – numeric input with stepper arrows.
- `submit` – a button that submits the form.

```html
<input type="text" placeholder="Your name">
```
The `placeholder` attribute provides a hint that disappears when typing.

quizData.question: Which `<input>` type masks the characters as you type?
quizData.explanation: `type="password"` hides the entered characters for privacy.

slides.title: Labels: Connecting Text to Inputs 🏷️
slides.content:
# The `<label>` Element

Every input should have a `<label>`. It makes the form accessible and increases the clickable area.

Two ways to associate a label with an input:
1. **Implicit:** wrap the input inside the label.
   ```html
   <label>Name: <input type="text"></label>
   ```
2. **Explicit:** use `for` attribute matching the input's `id`.
   ```html
   <label for="email">Email:</label>
   <input type="email" id="email">
   ```
The explicit method is preferred for styling flexibility.

slides.title: A Simple Login Form
slides.codeSnippet:
<form action="/login" method="post">
  <label for="username">Username:</label>
  <input type="text" id="username" name="username">
  
  <label for="password">Password:</label>
  <input type="password" id="password" name="password">
  
  <button type="submit">Log In</button>
</form>

quizData.question: It's fine to omit a `<label>` if you have a `placeholder` attribute.
quizData.explanation: `placeholder` is not a substitute for a label; labels provide persistent, accessible descriptions for screen readers.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## `name` is How Data Travels

The `name` attribute on form controls is crucial: it becomes the key when submitting data to a server. Without it, the input's value won't be sent.
